speaker: Doctor
text:
I am Dr. Agent. Please describe when you first noticed the double vision and whether your difficulty climbing stairs has been getting worse over time.

REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count (CBC), Creatine Kinase (CK), and Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies.
REQUEST IMAGES: MRI Brain, MRI Cervical Spine.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Acetylcholine_Receptor_Antibodies: Present (elevated); CBC: NORMAL READINGS; Creatine_Kinase (CK): NORMAL READINGS; MRI Brain: NORMAL READINGS; MRI Cervical Spine: NORMAL READINGS

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Tuberculosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is concerning; please clarify if you currently have any cough, night sweats, or weight loss, as those are key symptoms of Tuberculosis. Additionally, could you confirm if your difficulty climbing stairs involves your legs specifically, or if it is due to generalized fatigue? Your earlier mention of "double vision" and "symmetrical weakness" in all four limbs combined with a previous TB diagnosis suggests we need to rule out both neuromuscular junction disorders like Myasthenia Gravis and central causes like a brainstem stroke or tumor.

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had trouble swallowing or slurred speech. I also have not noticed breathing difficulty, and the symptoms started gradually about a month ago.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the gradual onset, symmetrical weakness in all four limbs, and double vision without bulbar symptoms (swallowing/speech), Tuberculosis is unlikely. While Myasthenia Gravis causes double vision and weakness, it typically worsens with fatigue and often affects eye movements more severely than limb strength. The combination of ocular symptoms and proximal limb weakness could also suggest a neuromuscular junction disorder like Lambert-Eaton or an inflammatory myopathy like polymyositis. Do you notice any improvement in your strength after resting for a short period? Also, have you experienced any recent muscle aches or rash?

speaker: Patient
text: The weakness is clearly worse with exertion and better after rest. I have not noticed muscle wasting or weight loss.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis. The fluctuating weakness that worsens with exertion and improves with rest, combined with diplopia (double vision) and the absence of sensory changes or bulbar symptoms, is the classic presentation of this neuromuscular junction disorder. The negative AChR antibody test I requested might be a false negative, as it occurs in about 50% of generalized cases; a repetitive nerve stimulation test or single-fiber EMG would confirm the diagnosis.
